title: Connecting to MongoDB Atlas
idea: MongoDB Atlas is MongoDB's hosted service. Your app reaches a cluster, a set of MongoDB servers Atlas runs for you, through one connection string.
points: Create a cluster in Atlas: the servers that will hold your databases.
Create a database user. It is separate from your Atlas login.
Add your IP address to the IP access list; only listed addresses connect.
Copy the connection string and store it, with the real password, in `MONGO_URI`.

hero.title: An Atlas connection string, part by part

parts.label: Scheme
parts.note: `+srv` makes the driver look up the cluster's servers in DNS, and enables TLS, so traffic is encrypted.

parts.label: Credentials
parts.note: A database user, not your Atlas login. Percent-encode special characters such as `@` in the password.

parts.label: Host
parts.note: The cluster's address, which Atlas generates. With `+srv` you give one host and no port.

parts.label: Database
parts.note: The database your app uses. Mongoose takes its name from here; the `dbName` option overrides it.

code.title: Keep it in the environment
code.caption: Placeholders only. Node 20 can load such a file: `node --env-file=.env app.mjs`.

code.title: Connect, and fail cleanly
code.caption: Mongoose, the library of the next page, connects here. This runs on a local MongoDB; Atlas changes only the string. A refused or blocked connection rejects, so catch it.

pitfalls: Never commit the connection string: it contains a password. Keep it in the environment.
A password with `@`, `/` or `:` breaks the string unless you percent-encode it.
The right password still fails if your IP is not on the access list.

quiz.why: The path after the host names the database. `%40` is an encoded `@`, so decoding the password gives `s@fe`.

takeaway: Atlas needs a user, an allowed IP and one connection string in the environment.
